approvalRequirements: Own or install a qualifying renewable energy source device whose components fall within Florida's statutory definition; ordinary HVAC equipment or controls qualify only when integral to the renewable device.
Meet the applicable installation-date, use, ownership, and assessment conditions for the residential assessment exclusion or the nonresidential tangible-personal-property exemption.

Report the property on any required county property or tangible-personal-property filing and provide permits, invoices, specifications, interconnection records, and other documentation requested by the county property appraiser.
Receive the county property appraiser's determination that the claimed property qualifies for the assessment reduction or exemption.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: Florida's treatment is statutory and noncompetitive. A documented device that satisfies the statutory technology and date rules is likely to receive the applicable assessment treatment after county review, but the broad retrofit mapping does not make standalone conventional HVAC or controls eligible.
reviews.evidenceText: Florida law excludes qualifying renewable-device value from residential assessment and exempts 80 percent of qualifying nonresidential tangible personal property. The definition includes specified solar, storage, geothermal, biogas, and integral control or heat-exchange components, with entitlement determined through property-tax administration.

approvalRequirements: Own taxable property containing a solar electric system in North Carolina.
Limit the claim to equipment used directly and exclusively to convert solar energy into electricity, as required by the statutory exclusion.
Submit Form AV-10 or the otherwise applicable property-tax exclusion filing to the county assessor for the relevant tax year.
Provide ownership, equipment, value, installation, and other supporting records requested by the assessor and receive approval of the exclusion.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: The 80 percent exclusion is a noncompetitive statutory benefit. A timely and complete claim for equipment that meets the direct-and-exclusive solar-electric test is likely to be approved after routine county assessment review.
reviews.evidenceText: North Carolina General Statutes exclude 80 percent of the appraised value of qualifying solar electric systems. The Department of Revenue's current AV-10 process includes the solar-electric exclusion and routes the claim through the county assessor.

approvalRequirements: Construct or install a qualifying active solar energy system before the current statutory sunset date.

Use the system for solar electricity, solar water or space conditioning, or another covered active-solar function; storage must be related to a qualifying solar-electric system rather than standalone storage.
Obtain required permits and retain system, cost, installation, and ownership records for the county assessor.
Submit a claim only when the limited initial-purchaser or builder-sale procedure applies; most additions to existing property do not require a separate claim form.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: California treats qualifying active-solar construction as excluded from new-construction assessment rather than as a competitive award. A system completed within the current eligibility period is likely to receive the exclusion, although the approaching January 1, 2027 sunset and transaction-specific first-purchaser rules require current confirmation.
reviews.evidenceText: The State Board of Equalization describes the benefit as a new-construction exclusion for qualifying active solar systems, generally administered without a claim when added to existing property. Solar-related storage can qualify, while passive systems, pool heating, wind equipment, and standalone storage are outside the stated scope.

approvalRequirements: Own qualifying renewable-energy equipment used in an exempt residential or manufacturing setting, or satisfy the municipality's current treatment for a commercial renewable facility.
Meet the statutory in-service, technology, ownership, and use conditions for the relevant property class.
Provide the municipality or tax assessor with interconnection approval, final authorization, program-enrollment records, equipment details, and other required reports.
Receive the local assessor's classification under the statewide exemption or the municipality's renewable-energy tax ordinance.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: Rhode Island law provides clear exemptions for specified residential and manufacturing renewable equipment, but commercial facilities may be taxed under municipality-specific rules. The target's conventional HVAC mapping is also unsupported unless the equipment is part of a qualifying renewable system, so approval is project- and locality-dependent.
reviews.evidenceText: Current Rhode Island law exempts specified residential renewable systems and qualifying manufacturing equipment. State rules require municipal reporting and permit local commercial renewable-energy taxation or waiver, making local classification material to the outcome.

approvalRequirements: Own or operate a qualifying renewable generation facility using an eligible source and, for solar, biomass, or landfill-gas facilities, meet the statutory minimum nameplate-capacity and installation-date rules.
Limit the property-tax exemption to equipment directly used in the eligible generation facility and covered by the replacement nameplate-capacity tax system.
File the annual nameplate-capacity report with the Nebraska Department of Revenue by the statutory deadline and provide facility, capacity, ownership, and operating information.
Pay the applicable nameplate-capacity tax and satisfy any Department or county verification requirements.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: Nebraska's exemption and replacement tax are formulaic rather than competitive. An eligible biomass or other covered generation facility that meets the capacity rules, files the required report, and pays the replacement tax is likely to receive the property-tax treatment.
reviews.evidenceText: Nebraska exempts qualifying renewable-generation property that is subject to the nameplate-capacity tax. Current Revenue guidance requires an annual facility report and administration of the replacement tax rather than a competitive incentive selection.

approvalRequirements: Own qualifying residential property with a new or refitted geothermal heating or cooling system installed on or after the statutory eligibility date.
File the geothermal property-tax exemption application with the county assessor by February 1 of the first assessment year for which the exemption is requested.
Provide installation date, equipment, cost, ownership, and residential-use documentation requested by the assessor.
Receive the assessor's approval; standalone battery storage is not established as eligible under the verified current geothermal exemption.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: The verified Iowa benefit is a ten-year, noncompetitive value exemption for qualifying residential geothermal systems. A timely first-year filing with adequate installation records is likely to be approved, but the legacy opportunity's battery-storage mapping was not substantiated.
reviews.evidenceText: Current Iowa tax guidance and assessor materials describe a ten-year property-value exemption for qualifying residential geothermal systems and a February 1 first-year filing deadline. The reviewed official materials do not establish a comparable standalone battery exemption under this opportunity.

approvalRequirements: Fit the property and equipment within a current Connecticut statutory category, such as qualifying Class I renewable equipment used for private residential or farm purposes, eligible solar heating equipment, or residential electric-vehicle charging equipment.
Meet the applicable installation-date, ownership, use, generation, and site-load restrictions for that category.
File the municipality's exemption claim or personal-property declaration as required and provide permits, invoices, specifications, interconnection records, and use documentation.
Receive the local assessor's eligibility determination for the specific statutory exemption.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: Connecticut's qualifying exemptions are statutory and noncompetitive, so a documented system within an enumerated category is likely to be approved. The legacy record is broader than the current categories, however, and does not establish eligibility for generic submetering or every mapped fuel-cell, biomass, or geothermal installation.
reviews.evidenceText: The current Connecticut legislative report identifies property-tax exemptions for specified residential or farm renewable systems, solar heating equipment, and residential EV charging equipment, each subject to statutory use and installation conditions and local assessment administration.

approvalRequirements: Install a qualifying renewable-energy system on residential, commercial, or industrial property in New Jersey.
Obtain certification of the system from the local enforcing agency or other authorized code official.
File Form CRES and the required certification and system documentation with the municipal tax assessor.
Receive assessor approval of the limited renewable-energy-system exemption.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: New Jersey uses an objective certification-and-assessor process rather than competitive selection. A qualifying renewable system with local code certification and a complete CRES filing is likely to receive the exemption, while conventional HVAC qualifies only when it is part of a covered renewable system.
reviews.evidenceText: The New Jersey Division of Taxation currently directs owners of qualifying renewable-energy systems to obtain local enforcing-agency certification and file Form CRES with the municipal assessor for the limited property-tax exemption.

approvalRequirements: For the verified exemption, have an independently owned residential solar electric generation facility located on residential property and installed on the customer's side of the meter.
Do not use the exempt facility to produce income other than the statutory utility rebates, offsets, credits, or reimbursements that are disregarded for this purpose.
Provide ownership, meter location, system, and income-use information to the county assessor if requested for classification.

Do not assume that a ground-source heat pump, community-solar subscription, biomass system, or standalone battery receives this property-tax exemption; those mapped measures were not established by the current exemption text.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: The verified current exemption is narrow and concerns independently owned residential solar electric property. None of the mapped target measures is that property type, and current law reviewed for this audit does not support a blanket exemption for the mapped geothermal, community-solar, biomass, or standalone-storage measures.
reviews.evidenceText: Colorado Revised Statutes exempt independently owned residential solar electric generation facilities from property tax when they are not used to produce income. The verified section does not create a general residential renewable-equipment exemption for the technologies mapped to this record.

approvalRequirements: Own residential property containing qualifying solar energy property or residential wind energy property.
Use the solar property to generate electricity, provide hot water, or perform another function within the statutory definition.
Retain permits, equipment specifications, installation records, and ownership documentation for local assessment administration.
Do not treat standalone submetering or energy-monitoring equipment as eligible solar or wind property.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: Maryland law directly excludes qualifying residential solar and wind property from real-property tax without a competitive award process. Once the property meets the statutory definition, the exemption is expected to apply through ordinary assessment administration.
reviews.evidenceText: Maryland's current statute states that residential solar energy property and residential wind energy property are not subject to real property tax. Solar energy property includes equipment that uses solar energy to generate electricity or provide hot water.

approvalRequirements: Operate a qualifying wind, solar, or geothermal energy-producing facility that is subject to Idaho's operating-property and gross-earnings tax rules.
File the annual operator statement with the Idaho State Tax Commission by April 30 and report the required property, generation, and gross-earnings information.
Provide additional records requested by the Commission and pay the substitute gross-earnings tax.
Do not assume that an ordinary building ground-source heat pump is an eligible geothermal energy producer.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: The current Idaho treatment applies to energy producers and substitutes a gross-earnings tax for property tax. The mapped ground-source building heat pump ordinarily is not an energy-producing facility, so the named benefit is unlikely for the target retrofit even though qualifying producers have a defined filing route.
reviews.evidenceText: The Idaho State Tax Commission administers wind, solar, and geothermal producers as operating property and requires annual operator statements. The regime is for energy-producing facilities, not a general exemption for building geothermal heat pumps.

approvalRequirements: Be an eligible PSE&G business customer, including an eligible nonprofit or public-sector facility, and meet the current small- or medium-facility usage thresholds for the selected Direct Install tier.
Submit program intake information and complete the no-cost on-site energy assessment.
Accept a program-approved scope, customer cost share, and any selected interest-free on-bill repayment terms before installation.
Use the program's authorized installation process for qualifying lighting, HVAC, refrigeration, motor, control, or other approved efficiency measures.
Complete installation, permits, invoices, inspection, and final PSE&G verification before the incentive is finalized.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: The current Direct Install successor program uses published customer-size, assessment, measure, and cost-share rules rather than competitive scoring. An eligible nonprofit or public facility that accepts the approved scope and completes verification is likely to receive the utility-funded share.
reviews.evidenceText: PSE&G currently offers no-cost assessments and utility-funded Direct Install projects for eligible small and midsized businesses, nonprofits, municipalities, schools, and other public-service customers. Project approval, customer cost share, installation, and final verification precede completion of the incentive.

approvalRequirements: Be a current PSE&G residential electric or gas customer, as applicable, and own an eligible existing single-family or one-to-four-unit attached home.
Use a participating contractor for HVAC, heat-pump, whole-home, or other contractor-delivered pathways that require one.
Install equipment that meets the current measure-specific efficiency, sizing, product-list, and fuel requirements.
Complete the instant-rebate acknowledgment or post-purchase claim and provide invoices, model information, and other requested records.
Permit random or required inspection; household appliance pathways do not establish eligibility for commercial refrigeration equipment or commercial dishwashers mapped to the legacy record.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: Current residential HVAC and appliance rebates are prescriptive and generally delivered through participating contractors or documented claims. A qualifying household project is likely to receive the rebate, but the record's commercial-refrigeration and commercial-dishwasher mappings are not supported by the residential offering.
reviews.evidenceText: PSE&G currently lists residential heating, cooling, heat-pump, thermostat, whole-home, and household-appliance incentives with participating-contractor or claim documentation and possible inspection. The residential pages do not substantiate commercial food-service or commercial refrigeration measures.

approvalRequirements: Maintain an eligible PSE&G electric account in good standing at the charging location and use the residential, commercial Level 2, or public DC fast-charging pathway that matches the site.
Use eligible smart Level 2 equipment or qualifying public DC fast-charging equipment and satisfy the applicable port, networking, access, and tariff requirements.
Use a New Jersey licensed electrician or other qualified contractor, obtain permits, and pass final electrical inspection.
Submit the online application with charger invoice, electrician invoice, serial number, inspection or permit records, site information, and any engineering documentation.
Complete PSE&G eligibility, engineering, document, and data-sharing review; the incentive generally supports customer-side make-ready work rather than purchase of the charger itself.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: PSE&G publishes objective residential, commercial Level 2, and public DC fast-charging make-ready pathways. A conforming project with complete invoices, permits, inspection, and utility review is likely to receive the applicable credit, subject to program limits and available funding.
reviews.evidenceText: PSE&G's current EV programs require an eligible account, qualified charging equipment, licensed electrical work, permits and inspection, invoices, online application, and utility review. Residential, commercial Level 2, and public DC fast-charging projects use separate make-ready pathways.

approvalRequirements: Be an eligible PSEG Long Island business customer with the project installed at a served commercial facility.
Select a currently supported lighting, HVAC, refrigeration, weatherization, motor, drive, or other commercial-efficiency measure and meet its technical specifications.
Submit the application, project scope, equipment data, and estimated savings and receive written preapproval before purchasing equipment or beginning installation.
Complete the preapproved work and submit final invoices, product documentation, and completion records within the approval period.
Pass any required post-installation inspection or savings verification before payment.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: The commercial program is prescriptive or custom rather than competitively ranked, but current materials require project preapproval. An eligible customer that obtains approval before commitment and completes the approved scope with full documentation is likely to receive the rebate.
reviews.evidenceText: PSEG Long Island currently requires preapproval for commercial efficiency projects and lists incentives across lighting, HVAC, refrigeration, weatherization, and other categories. Final payment follows installation records and any required verification.

approvalRequirements: Be a current PSEG Long Island residential customer at the installation address.
Purchase or install a measure that appears in the current residential rebate catalog and meets its equipment, sizing, efficiency, fuel, and installation requirements.
Use a participating contractor for heat-pump, whole-home, or other pathways that require one; complete an assessment when required by the selected pathway.
Submit the measure-specific application, invoice, model information, and installation records within the published purchase and filing deadlines.
Allow PSEG Long Island to verify customer, product, contractor, and installation eligibility before payment.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: PSEG Long Island maintains active, objective residential pathways for heat pumps, water heating, thermostats, selected appliances, and assessments. A complete claim or participating-contractor submission for a current measure is likely to be paid after routine eligibility review.
reviews.evidenceText: Current PSEG Long Island residential pages publish measure-specific customer, equipment, contractor, purchase-date, documentation, and filing rules. Assessments and participating contractors are required only for the pathways that specify them and do not make an otherwise qualifying award competitive.

approvalRequirements: Apply during an open Efficiency Maine charging-infrastructure solicitation and use the technology and site type covered by that round.
For the current Level 2 round, propose an eligible Maine priority site with at least four networked charging ports and document site control or an owner-host agreement.
Commit to the required public availability, operating term, networking, maintenance, accessibility, and federal funding conditions.
Submit a complete competitive proposal with technical design, budget, cost-share, schedule, organizational records, certifications, and required forms.
Be selected through proposal evaluation, execute the grant agreement, complete construction and commissioning, and satisfy reporting and reimbursement requirements.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: Efficiency Maine's public-charger funding is issued through periodic competitive solicitations rather than an entitlement. A current Level 2 round is available, but proposals are evaluated and funding is limited; the previously reviewed DC fast-charging round is not an open general award path.
reviews.evidenceText: Efficiency Maine currently administers public charging grants through technology- and location-specific requests for proposals. The active Level 2 solicitation requires a competitive proposal, eligible public sites and ports, long-term operating commitments, cost documentation, and a grant agreement; DC fast-charging availability is round-dependent.

approvalRequirements: Be a Public Service Company of Oklahoma residential electric customer at the installation address.
Purchase an ENERGY STAR certified Level 2 electric-vehicle charger that meets the current product requirements.
Submit the online rebate application within 45 days of purchase and provide the receipt, model information, account details, and other requested documentation.
Receive PSO's customer, product, purchase-date, and documentation approval while rebate funds remain available.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: PSO publishes a fixed, prescriptive residential Level 2 charger rebate with a short filing deadline. A current customer with an eligible ENERGY STAR charger and complete timely proof is likely to receive the rebate after routine claim review.
reviews.evidenceText: PSO's current offer provides a residential rebate for an ENERGY STAR certified Level 2 charger and requires an online application and purchase documentation within 45 days. The claim is administrative rather than competitively scored.

approvalRequirements: Obtain and maintain Puerto Rico Bona Fide Farmer certification or an applicable agricultural tax-exemption decree.
Meet the qualifying agricultural-income or new-farmer requirements and document the covered agricultural operation.

Use the claimed equipment in the covered agricultural activity and satisfy the statutory equipment-use condition, including sole dependence on solar, wind, hydraulic, or another nonpetroleum energy source where that category is claimed.
Present the valid exempt-purchase certificate for each qualifying transaction and retain invoices and use records for Treasury review.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: Act 60 provides a rules-based tax exemption for certified bona fide farmers purchasing listed equipment for covered agricultural activities. A certified farmer that documents qualifying use and presents the required transaction certificate is likely to receive the exemption; a solar water-heating system must actually fit the statutory energy-equipment and agricultural-use conditions.
reviews.evidenceText: Puerto Rico's current Incentives Code exempts specified purchases by bona fide farmers and requires certification, qualifying agricultural activity and income, proof of equipment use, and an exempt-purchase certificate for each transaction. Covered energy equipment includes systems operating solely from qualifying nonpetroleum energy sources.

approvalRequirements: Establish or propose an eligible Puerto Rico manufacturing business or commercial green-energy business within the current Incentives Code.
File an incentive-decree application with the Department of Economic Development and Commerce and provide ownership, activity, investment, employment, financial, site, and project information.
Show that the biomass or biogas activity and claimed property are used in the eligible business rather than merely being an isolated retrofit at an otherwise ineligible facility.
Receive agency evaluation and an executed decree, then satisfy permits, reporting, employment, investment, and other decree-specific compliance conditions.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: The current Puerto Rico incentives are decree-based and depend on the applicant's qualifying business activity and economic contribution, not solely on installing biomass equipment. Approval is discretionary and project-specific, so an unreviewed retrofit has only a possible award path.
reviews.evidenceText: Act 60 provides tax incentives through DDEC decrees for eligible manufacturing and commercial green-energy businesses. Applications are evaluated using business, investment, employment, property-use, and economic-contribution information, and the decree controls the available benefits.

approvalRequirements: Conduct an eligible commercial green-energy activity in Puerto Rico, such as qualifying renewable-energy production, sale, equipment activity, or an eligible energy-storage business.
Submit a complete green-energy incentive-decree application to DDEC with project, ownership, financing, site, capacity, technology, employment, and economic-contribution information.

Show that the real or movable property for which the exemption is claimed is used in the activity covered by the decree; biomass, biogas, and storage must meet the current statutory definitions and scale conditions.
Receive the decree and coordinate the approved property-tax treatment with CRIM, then maintain required reporting and continuing decree compliance.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: The current successor benefit is a decree-based partial property-tax exemption for qualifying commercial green-energy businesses, not an automatic blanket exemption for any renewable device. Eligibility and approval depend on business scale, statutory definitions, agency review, and decree terms.
reviews.evidenceText: Puerto Rico's current Incentives Code provides a 75 percent property-tax exemption for qualifying property used in a green-energy activity covered by a DDEC decree. The law defines eligible renewable and storage businesses and requires application, evaluation, and continuing compliance.

approvalRequirements: Limit the exemption to qualifying electric solar equipment used to produce or store electricity and necessary accessories or components.
Have the importer, distributor, or manufacturer submit the technical certifications required by Hacienda, including compliance with applicable energy standards and the minimum warranty documentation.
Obtain Hacienda's administrative determination approving the equipment for exempt treatment.
Use the required SURI import, sales, and exemption documentation for the transaction and retain product and warranty records.
Do not assume that a solar thermal water-heating system qualifies under the verified electric-solar-equipment exemption.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: The current Hacienda procedure covers electric solar equipment for producing or storing electricity. The mapped retrofit is solar water heating, which is not established as eligible under that electric-equipment exemption, so an award under this opportunity is unlikely without a separate current authority.
reviews.evidenceText: Hacienda's current circular requires supplier technical certifications, warranty documentation, and an administrative determination for electric solar equipment used to produce or store electricity. The reviewed procedure does not substantiate solar thermal water-heating equipment.

approvalRequirements: Be a current Puget Sound Energy electric or natural-gas customer and own or manage an eligible multifamily property with at least five attached dwelling units or another currently qualifying multifamily configuration.
Complete the program's eligibility assessment before making improvements and provide site, account, building, equipment, and energy-use information.
Apply for and receive preapproval before purchasing or installing measures when directed by the current multifamily process.
Install measures that meet current technical, contractor, product-list, fuel, and site requirements.
Submit invoices, equipment records, and completion documentation and pass any required post-installation inspection before payment.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: PSE's current multifamily program uses a defined assessment and preapproval process rather than competitive ranking. An eligible property with an approved scope, qualifying installation, and complete closeout documentation is likely to receive the applicable rebate.
reviews.evidenceText: Puget Sound Energy currently directs eligible multifamily customers to complete an assessment and apply for preapproval before improvements. The program lists measure-specific rebates and requires qualifying installation, invoices, and verification for payment.

approvalRequirements: Be a current Puget Sound Energy customer and meet the home, ownership or occupancy, fuel, and existing-building conditions for the selected residential offer.
Install equipment or weatherization that meets the current measure-specific performance, product, and sizing rules.
Use a PSE Recommended Energy Professional or other approved contractor when required for weatherization, windows, HVAC, or instant-rebate delivery.
Complete the instant-rebate acknowledgment or submit the post-installation claim with invoices, model numbers, efficiency ratings, and required forms within the published deadline.
Permit inspection or verification and confirm that a generic energy-management system is eligible only when it falls within a currently listed thermostat or control measure.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: PSE's current residential rebates are objective, measure-specific offerings delivered through approved contractors or documented claims. A qualifying installation submitted on time is likely to be paid after routine review, while the broad legacy mapping does not establish every generic control or equipment category.
reviews.evidenceText: Puget Sound Energy currently publishes residential heating, water-heating, weatherization, and window rebates with measure-specific customer, contractor, equipment, invoice, and deadline requirements. Payment follows instant-rebate processing or post-installation claim verification.

approvalRequirements: Own qualifying real property or fixtures within an energy facility whose aggregate nameplate capacity is 250 kilowatts or less.
Have the qualifying facility completed on or after January 1, 2010 and use an energy resource covered by the current statutory definition.
Maintain capacity, completion-date, ownership, and facility records and provide them to the county auditor or other tax authority if requested for assessment administration.
Do not seek the separate state certification required for larger projects under a different Ohio statute; the small-project exemption is statutory.
reviews.awardLikelihoodReason: Ohio law directly exempts qualifying property in energy facilities of 250 kilowatts or less that meet the completion-date rule. A qualifying small wind project should receive the exemption through ordinary assessment administration rather than competitive or discretionary program selection.
reviews.evidenceText: Ohio Revised Code section 5709.53 exempts qualifying real property and fixtures within an energy facility with aggregate nameplate capacity of 250 kilowatts or less when the facility satisfies the statutory completion-date requirement. The section does not require the state certification used for larger projects.
